content.text: The verifier's narrative confirms the classification; the only failing item is a deterministic "audit frequency limited" check that cannot be satisfied because there is no audit clause to parametrize. I'll resubmit the compliant finding with that inapplicability stated explicitly, and without any redline (correct for a compliant finding).

input.quote: IBM reserves the right to investigate potential violations of the representations and warranties in Subsection 11.2(b). If IBM reasonably determines that a breach of any such warranty has occurred, then IBM may, in its sole and reasonable discretion:
input.rationale:
No audit right binds the Customer anywhere in this Agreement, so our position is better than the AUDIT preferred position and the clause set is compliant with no redline.

Evidence: searches for "audit", "inspect", "verify", "monitor" and "premises" return no hits; "records" appears only in the § 9.1 liability carve-out for loss of records or data. The sections that could host a usage-verification right contain none — § 4.1 Charges / § 4.2 Payment, § 11.5 Capacity Planning (allocates capacity-planning responsibility to Customer only), § 12.1 License (copying/reverse-engineering restrictions only), § 13.2 Acceptable Use Policy (IBM modification right on 30 days' notice) and §§ 14.1–14.20.

The planner's candidate hook, § 11.3, is a breach-remedy provision, not an audit right: IBM may investigate suspected breaches of the § 11.2(b) content/acceptable-use warranties and then restrict access to the Services, require removal of Content, terminate for cause or pursue other remedies (p0132–p0136), with an undertaking to attempt notice before restricting access or removing Content (p0137). It confers no right of access to Bluefly's systems, personnel, books or records, no remote access, and no audit cost or cooperation burden on us. There is therefore nothing to parametrize with frequency, notice, independent-auditor, cost-shifting or no-system-access limits.

Inapplicable deterministic check: the "audit frequency limited" test fails only because no audit clause exists to carry a frequency cap. That is an artifact of absence, not a material failure — the walk-away triggers (unlimited or unannounced audits, remote access to Customer systems) are not met because no audit or access right is granted at all. Inserting frequency/notice/cost language would manufacture an audit right in IBM's favour that it does not currently hold, contrary to our interest as customer.

Residual observation, noted rather than flagged: § 11.3's investigation right is uncapped in frequency and its notice commitment is best-efforts ("will attempt to notify") with emergency and legal-requirement carve-outs. As a minor sub-element of a remedy clause that involves no entry into our environment, we would leave it as drafted; if § 11.3 is later expanded to include access to Customer records or systems, this rule should be re-run against it.
